concept.name: Look-ahead bias
concept.definition: A backtesting error in which a simulated decision uses information that would not have been available at the simulated decision time, such as future prices, revised fundamentals, or full-sample statistics, artificially inflating measured performance.
concept.intuition: It is trading with tomorrow's newspaper: any rule looks brilliant if at each historical date it quietly consults data that only became known later.
concept.mechanics: Common forms include signals computed on a bar's close but executed at that same close, use of revised rather than point-in-time fundamentals, universes defined with hindsight, and features normalized with full-sample means and variances. Prevention requires point-in-time data, lagging signal computation relative to execution, and walk-forward rather than full-sample preprocessing.
concept.failure_modes: Subtle leaks, index membership, delisting returns, feature scaling, and cross-validation folds that interleave past and future, survive casual review and almost always bias results upward, making weak strategies appear strong.
concept.misconceptions: That look-ahead bias requires explicitly using future prices: standard i.i.d. cross-validation on autocorrelated financial data leaks future information through overlapping folds just as surely.
concept.example: A moving-average crossover computed with a centered window uses prices after the signal date; switching to a trailing window with next-open execution removes several percent of phantom annual return.

citations.source: Bailey, Borwein, Lopez de Prado and Zhu (2014), 'Pseudo-mathematics and Financial Charlatanism', Notices of the AMS 61(5):458-471
